title: Bears explode for 59 points in record-setting win over Panthers. Can they keep it up?
author: Kevin Fishbain
content:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — The Chicago Bears outslugged the Carolina Panthers 59-37 in the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history Sunday at Bank of America Stadium.

With 96 combined points, the Bears and Panthers shattered the previous mark for an opener — the 88 points posted in a 48-40 Tampa Bay win over New Orleans in 2018. The Bears set a franchise record for points in an opener, besting a 45-7 win over the Packers in 1948.

Quarterback Caleb Williams led the Bears to eight touchdowns. He passed for two and rushed for two. Running back D’Andre Swift also rushed for three scores, and Kyle Monangai had a 61-yard TD run. The Bears racked up 552 total yards, 291 on the ground.

Bryce Young threw three touchdown passes to lead the Panthers, including two to receiver Jalen Coker, who finished with eight catches for 138 yards.

Box score | Week 1 live blog | Game discussion

This wasn’t just a road blowout. This was a warning to the rest of the NFC that the Bears are loaded with firepower and operating with the mindset of their uber-confident and greedy head coach, Ben Johnson. Admittedly, the sample size is small, but it sure seems like this group is going to be a load to handle.

Swift, just two days after signing a three-year, $33.75 million contract extension, contributed 134 total yards and three TDs, as the Bears showed incredible balance while producing a flood of explosive plays.

“Caleb came out pretty hot in this game,” Johnson said. “But I think really when you look at the stat sheet, the story of the game ended up being the rushing. Offensive line, shout-out to them. But it was collective with the tight ends, the receivers were blocking their tails off as well. And Swifty and Monongai both were able to do a great job there. Caleb added quite a bit with his feet also.”

Williams, in his second season working with Johnson, completed 21 of his 29 passes for 269 yards with two touchdowns and added 65 rushing yards, including TDs from 9 and 29 yards. And somehow, it didn’t feel like Williams was even close to his best.

The Bears totaled 26 first downs. The offense didn’t even seem to be clicking in the first half and still found its way to 319 yards and 31 points.

“It was wild. It really was,” tight end Cole Kmet said. “When we came in at halftime, it honestly felt like we had left some stuff out there. And we still had 31 (points). Kind of a different thing to be part of. Which is fun.”

Sunday’s leading receiver: Kalif Raymond (eight catches, 84 yards). Ascending young tight end Colston Loveland, meanwhile, went without a catch. Imagine the potency when the Bears get him heated up. — Dan Wiederer

For the Bears, the easy reaction to this win is that they might have to score 50 points every week to help out a defense that allowed 31 points in three quarters. There were a few bright spots, like Montez Sweat’s third-down sack, Malik Muhammad’s end-of-half interception and Jaylon Johnson’s forced fumble, which linebacker Devin Bush recovered. But the pass rush was lacking. Sweat and Kentavius Street each had a sack and a QB hit — the Bears got only one other quarterback hit in the first three-and-a-half quarters.

They struggled mightily covering Coker, who went over 100 yards, including a 51-yard score past cornerback Tyrique Stevenson. It’s the first game of the season, the secondary is missing a couple of starters, there are new players up front — all the caveats are there, but the biggest concern from last year’s team still lingers, and probably will in several games this season. The good news is they got a couple of takeaways, their calling card from 2025, but not something they can count on week in and week out. They’ll need more from the pass rush. — Kevin Fishbain

The Panthers’ defensive meltdown was concerning at every level because defense was supposed to be the team’s biggest area of improvement after Carolina spent big on edge rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebacker Devin Lloyd in free agency. After a promising start, with a takeaway on the Bears’ first possession, the wheels came off Ejiro Evero’s defense in a hurry.

By the end, the Panthers had allowed a team-record 59 points, tied for the 10th-most in a single game in the NFL since the 1970 merger.

“Fifty-nine is an ugly score to put up as a defense,” Phillips said. “It was embarrassing.”

They had no answer for Williams, who shredded Carolina with his arms and legs. Just as alarming was the inability to stop the Bears’ running attack. Including Williams’ scramble yards, the Bears had three rushers finish with at least 65 yards. The abysmal performance will immediately put Evero in the crosshairs of critics, especially if the Panthers struggle next week against an Atlanta team that started Cooper Rush at quarterback Sunday in Pittsburgh. — Joe Person

If there was a silver lining for the Panthers, it was the play of Young, who did his best to match Williams score for score. Young completed 23 of 37 passes for 361 yards and three touchdowns. Those were the second-most passing yards of his career, trailing only a 448-yard effort in an overtime win at Atlanta last year. Young had one interception, but it was in the final seconds of the first half when he was trying to make a play. Young dropped to 0-4 in season openers, but this loss falls squarely on the defense. Coker was another positive for the Panthers with his career-high 138 yards. — Person

Williams’ sneak attempt failed and set up the Panthers in plus territory to tie the game at 21-21. Johnson acknowledged he didn’t call a good game in the first half, but he didn’t apologize for that call.

“Listen, that’ll always be the goal is we want to be the highest-scoring (team),” he said. “We want to have the most wins. We want to win Super Bowls; that’s what we do. We didn’t get into this profession trying to be mediocre or average. And that’s every NFL team, so that is what it is. We make decisions over the course of a week about what’s best for our football team to win the game. That’s the most important thing and that goes into everything that we do. ” — Fishbain
